label: def:graded_set
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:graded_set}
\begin{enumerate}
\item An \textbf{($\mathbb{N}$-)graded set} $\Gamma$ is a family 
$\Gamma=(\Gamma_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of sets
indexed by natural numbers $\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$.
By an \textbf{element of $\Gamma$} we mean an element of the 
set $\coprod_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \Gamma_n=\{\,(n,\gamma)\mid n\in\mathbb{N}, \gamma\in 
\Gamma_n\,\}$.
We write $x\in\Gamma$ if $x$ is an element of $\Gamma$.
\item If $\Gamma=(\Gamma_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $\Gamma'=(\Gamma'_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$
are graded sets, then a \textbf{morphism of graded sets} $f\colon 
\Gamma\longrightarrow
\Gamma'$ is a family of functions $f=(f_n\colon \Gamma_n\longrightarrow 
\Gamma'_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$.\qedhere
\end{enumerate}

label: def:Sigma_term
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:Sigma_term}
Let $\Sigma$ be a graded set.
The graded set $T(\Sigma)=(T(\Sigma)_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of \textbf{$\Sigma$-terms}
is defined inductively as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and  $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$, 
\[
x_i^{(n)}\in T(\Sigma)_n.
\]
We sometimes omit the superscript and write $x_i$ for $x_i^{(n)}$.
\item For each $n,k\in\mathbb{N}$, $\sigma\in\Sigma_k$ and $t_1,\dots,t_k\in 
T(\Sigma)_n$,
\[
\sigma(t_1,\dots,t_k)\in T(\Sigma)_n.
\]
When $k=0$, we usually omit the parentheses in $\sigma()$
and write instead as $\sigma$.\qedhere
\end{enumerate}

label: def:interp_Sigma_term
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:interp_Sigma_term}
Let $\Sigma$ be a graded set and 
$(A,{[\![-]\!]})$ be a 
$\Sigma$-algebra.
We define the \textbf{interpretation} ${[\![-]\!]'}$ of $\Sigma$-terms
recursively as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$,
\[
{[\![x^{(n)}_i]\!]'}\colon A^n\longrightarrow A
\]
is the $i$-th projection $(a_1,\dots,a_n)\longmapsto a_i$.
\item For each $n,k\in\mathbb{N}$, $\sigma\in\Sigma_k$ and $t_1\dots,t_k\in 
T(\Sigma)_n$,
\[
{[\![\sigma(t_1,\dots,t_k)]\!]'}\colon A^n\longrightarrow A
\] 
maps $(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in A^n$ to 
${[\![\sigma]\!]}({[\![t_1]\!]'}(a_1,\dots,a_n),\dots,
{[\![t_k]\!]'}(a_1,\dots,a_n))$;
that is, ${[\![\sigma(t_1,\dots,t_k)]\!]'}$ is the following composite:
\[
\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline=-\the\dimexpr\fontdimen22\textfont2\relax ]
      \node (1) at (0,0)  {$A^n$};
      \node (2) at (3,0)  {$A^k$};
      \node (3) at (5,0) {$A.$};
       
      \draw[->] (1) to node[auto,labelsize]{$\langle 
      {[\![t_1]\!]'},\dots,{[\![t_k]\!]'}\rangle$} (2);
      \draw[->] (2) to node[auto,labelsize] {${[\![\sigma]\!]}$} (3);
       
\end{tikzpicture} 
\]
\end{enumerate}
Note that for any $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\sigma\in\Sigma_n$,
${[\![\sigma]\!]}={[\![\sigma(x^{(n)}_1,\dots,x^{(n)}_n)]\!]'}$.
Henceforth, for any $\Sigma$-term $t$
we simply write ${[\![t]\!]}$ for ${[\![t]\!]'}$ defined above.

Let $\Sigma$ be a graded set.
An element of the graded set $T(\Sigma)\times T(\Sigma)$ is called a 
\textbf{$\Sigma$-equation}.
We write a $\Sigma$-equation $(n,(t,s))\in T(\Sigma)\times T(\Sigma)$ (that is,
$n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $t,s\in T(\Sigma)_n$) as $t\approx_n s$ or $t\approx s$.

\label{def:semantical_consequence_rel}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Let $\Sigma$ be a graded set and 
$(A,{[\![-]\!]})$ be a $\Sigma$-algebra.
For any $\Sigma$-equation $t\approx_n s\in T(\Sigma)\times T(\Sigma)$, we write 
\[
(A,{[\![-]\!]})\vDash t\approx_n s
\]
to mean ${[\![t]\!]}={[\![s]\!]}$.
\item Let ${{\langle\, \Sigma\, |\, E \,\rangle}}$ be a presentation of an equational theory.
For any $\Sigma$-equation $t\approx_n s\in T(\Sigma)\times T(\Sigma)$, we write
\[
{{\langle\, \Sigma\, |\, E \,\rangle}}\vDash t\approx_n s
\] 
to mean that for any model 
$(A,{[\![-]\!]})$ of ${{\langle\, \Sigma\, |\, E \,\rangle}}$,
$(A,{[\![-]\!]})\vDash t\approx_n s$.\qedhere
\end{enumerate}

label: def:clone
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:clone}
A \textbf{clone} $\mathsf{T}$ consists of:
\begin{description}
\item[(CD1)] a graded set $T=(T_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$;
\item[(CD2)] for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$, an element
\[
p^{(n)}_i\in T_n;
\]
\item[(CD3)] for each $k,n\in\mathbb{N}$, a function
\[
\circ^{(n)}_k\colon T_k\times (T_n)^k\longrightarrow T_n
\]
whose action on an element $(\phi,\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k)\in T_k\times (T_n)^k$
we write as $\phi\circ^{(n)}_k(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k)$
or simply as $\phi\circ(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k)$;
\end{description}
satisfying the following equations:
\begin{description}
\item[(CA1)] for each $k,n\in\mathbb{N}$, $j\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ and 
$\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k\in T_n$, 
\[
p^{(k)}_j\circ^{(n)}_k(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k) = \theta_j;
\]
\item[(CA2)] for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $\theta\in T_n$,
\[
\theta\circ^{(n)}_n (p^{(n)}_1,\dots,p^{(n)}_n) = \theta;
\]
\item[(CA3)] for each $l,k,n\in\mathbb{N}$, $\psi\in T_l$, $\phi_1,\dots,\phi_l\in
T_k$, $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k\in T_n$, 
\begin{multline*}
\psi\circ^{(k)}_l\big(\phi_1\circ^{(n)}_k(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k),\ 
\dots,\ \phi_l\circ^{(n)}_k(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k)\big)
\\=
\big(\psi\circ^{(k)}_l(\phi_1,\dots,\phi_l)\big)\circ^{(n)}_k 
(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k).
\end{multline*}
\end{description}
Such a clone is written as 
$\mathsf{T}=(T,(p^{(i)}_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N},i\in\{1,\dots,n\}},
(\circ^{(n)}_k)_{k,n\in\mathbb{N}})$
or simply $(T,p,\circ)$.

title: Definition
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. The graded set ${\langle A, B\rangle}$ is defined by 
setting,
for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, ${\langle A, B\rangle}_n$ be the set of all functions from $A^n$
to $B$.
\item Let $A,A'$ and $B$ be sets and $f\colon A'\longrightarrow A$ be a 
function.
The morphism of graded sets 
${\langle f, B\rangle}\colon{\langle A, B\rangle}\longrightarrow{\langle A', B\rangle}$
is defined by setting, for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, 
${\langle f, B\rangle}_n\colon{\langle A, B\rangle}_n\longrightarrow{\langle A', B\rangle}_n$ be the 
precomposition by $f^n\colon (A')^n\longrightarrow A^n$;
that is, $h\longmapsto h\circ f^n$. 
\item Let $A,B$ and $B'$ be sets and $g\colon B\longrightarrow B'$ be a 
function.
The morphism of graded sets 
${\langle A, g\rangle}\colon{\langle A, B\rangle}\longrightarrow{\langle A, B'\rangle}$
is defined by setting, for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, 
${\langle A, g\rangle}_n\colon{\langle A, B\rangle}_n\longrightarrow{\langle A, B'\rangle}_n$ be the 
postcomposition by $g\colon B\longrightarrow B'$;
that is, $h\longmapsto g\circ h$.\qedhere
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
The clone homomorphism $g$ may be defined by using the inductive nature of 
the definition of $T(\Sigma)$, as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$, let
\[
g_n(x^{(n)}_i)=p^{(n)}_i;
\]
\item for each $k,n\in\mathbb{N}$, $\sigma\in\Sigma_k$ and $t_1,\dots,t_k\in 
T(\Sigma)_n$, let 
\[
g_n(\sigma(t_1,\dots,t_k))=f_k(\sigma)\circ^{(n)}_k(g_n(t_1),\dots,g_n(t_k)).
\]
\end{enumerate}
To check that $g$ is indeed a clone homomorphism, it suffices to show 
for each $s\in T(\Sigma)_k$ and $t_1,\dots,t_k\in T(\Sigma)_n$,
\[
g_n(s[x^{(k)}_1\mapsto t_1,\dots,x^{(k)}_k\mapsto t_k])=
g_k(s)\circ^{(n)}_k(g_n(t_1),\dots, g_n(t_k));
\]
this can be shown by induction on $s$.
The uniqueness of $g$ is clear.

body_md:
\label{def:streg_Sigma_term}
Let $\Sigma$ be a graded set.
The graded set $T_\mathrm{SR}(\Sigma)=(T_\mathrm{SR}(\Sigma)_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of 
\textbf{strongly regular $\Sigma$-terms} is defined inductively as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $x^{(1)}_1\in T_\mathrm{SR}(\Sigma)_1$.
\item For each $k,n_1,\dots,n_k\in\mathbb{N}$, $\sigma\in\Sigma_k$ and 
$t_1\in T_\mathrm{SR}(\Sigma)_{n_1},\dots,t_k\in T_\mathrm{SR}(\Sigma)_{n_k}$,
writing $n_1+\dots+n_k=n$,
\begin{multline*}
\sigma(t_1[x^{(n_1)}_1\mapsto x^{(n)}_1,\dots,x^{(n_1)}_{n_1}\mapsto 
x^{(n)}_{n_1}],
\dots,\\
t_k[x^{(n_k)}_1\mapsto x^{(n)}_{n_1+\dots+n_{k-1}+1},\dots,
x^{(n_k)}_{n_k}\mapsto x^{(n)}_{n_1+\dots+n_{k-1}+n_k}])
\in T_\mathrm{SR}(\Sigma)_{n}.
\end{multline*}
When $k=0$, we usually write $\sigma$ instead of $\sigma()$.\qedhere
\end{enumerate}

Homomorphisms between set or abelian group models of $\mathsf{T}$

label: def:symm_op
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:symm_op}
A \textbf{symmetric operad} $\mathsf{T}$ consists of:
\begin{description}
\item[(SD1)] a graded set $T=(T_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$;
\item[(SD2)] an element ${\mathrm{id}_{}}\in T_1$;
\item[(SD3)] for each $k,n_1,\dots,n_k\in\mathbb{N}$, a function
(we omit the sub- and superscripts)
\[
\circ\colon T_k\times T_{n_1}\times\dots\times T_{n_k}\longrightarrow
T_{n_1+\dots+n_k}
\]
whose action we write as $(\phi,\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k)\longmapsto
\phi\circ(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k)$;
\item[(SD4)] for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, a function
\[
\bullet\colon \mathfrak{S}_n\times T_n\longrightarrow T_n
\]
\end{description}
satisfying the following equations:
\begin{description}
\item[(SA1)] for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\theta\in T_n$,
\[
{\mathrm{id}_{}}\circ (\theta)=\theta;
\]
\item[(SA2)] for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\theta\in T_n$,
\[
\theta\circ ({\mathrm{id}_{}},\dots,{\mathrm{id}_{}}) = \theta;
\] 
\item[(SA3)] for each $l,\ k_1,\dots,k_l,\ 
n_{1,1},\dots,n_{1,k_1},\dots,n_{l,1},
\dots,n_{l,k_l}\in\mathbb{N}$, \ $\psi\in T_l$, \ $\phi_1\in T_{k_1}, \dots, \phi_l\in 
T_{k_l}$, \ $\theta_{1,1}\in T_{n_{1,1}},\dots,\theta_{1,k_1}\in T_{n_{1,k_1}},
\dots, \theta_{l,1}\in T_{n_{l,1}},\dots, \theta_{l,k_l}\in T_{n_{l, k_l}}$,
\begin{multline*}
\psi\circ\big(\phi_1\circ (\theta_{1,1},\dots,\theta_{1,k_1}),\ \dots\ ,
\phi_l\circ (\theta_{l,1},\dots,\theta_{l,k_l}) \big)\\
=
\big(\psi\circ 
(\phi_1,\dots,\phi_l)\big)\circ(\theta_{1,1},\dots,\theta_{1,k_1},\ \dots\ ,
\theta_{l,1},\dots,\theta_{l,k_l});
\end{multline*}
\item[(SA4)] for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, the function $\bullet\colon 
\mathfrak{S}_n\times T_n\longrightarrow T_n$ is a left group action, 
that is, for each $\theta\in T_n$ and $u,v\in \mathfrak{S}_n$, 
\[
e_n\bullet \theta =\theta, \quad
(v\cdot u)\bullet \theta=v\bullet(u\bullet\theta);
\]
\item[(SA5)] for each $k,n_1,\dots,n_k\in\mathbb{N}$, $\phi\in T_k$, $\theta_1\in 
T_{n_1},\dots,\theta_k\in T_{n_k}$ and $u_1\in\mathfrak{S}_{n_1},\dots,
u_k\in\mathfrak{S}_{n_k}$,
\[
\phi\circ(u_1\bullet\theta_1,\dots,u_k\bullet\theta_k)
=(u_1\oplus \dots\oplus u_k)\bullet\big(\phi\circ(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k)\big);
\]
\item[(SA6)] for each $k,n_1,\dots,n_k\in\mathbb{N}$, $\phi\in T_k$, $\theta_1\in 
T_{n_1},\dots,\theta_k\in T_{n_k}$ and $v\in\mathfrak{S}_k$,
\[
(v\bullet \phi)\circ(\theta_{v^{-1}(1)},\dots,\theta_{v^{-1}(k)})
=v_{n_1,\dots,n_k}\bullet \big(\phi\circ(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k)\big).\qedhere
\]
\end{description}

label: ex:non_symm_op_as_gen_op
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:non_symm_op_as_gen_op}
If we let $\mathcal{C}=\mathbf{Set}$ and $\mathsf{S}$ be the free monoid monad
(which is cartesian), 
then $\mathsf{S}$-operads are equivalent to {non-symmetric operads}.
The arities are the natural numbers: $S1\cong\mathbb{N}$.

In more detail, the data of an $\mathsf{S}$-operad in this case
consist of a set $T$, and functions 
${\mathrm{ar}_{T}}\colon T\longrightarrow \mathbb{N}$, $e\colon 1\longrightarrow T$
and $m\colon (T,{\mathrm{ar}_{T}})\ast T\longrightarrow T$. 
Unravelling this, we obtain a graded set $(T_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$, 
an element ${\mathrm{id}_{}}\in T_1$ and 
a family of functions $(m_{k,n_1,\dots n_k}\colon T_k\times T_{n_1}\times\dots
\times T_{n_k}
\longrightarrow 
T_{n_1+\dots +n_k})_{k,n_1,\dots,n_k\in\mathbb{N}}$,
agreeing with Definition~\ref{def:non_symm_op}.
Note that indeed $T_n$ may be interpreted as the set of all (derived) 
operations of arity $n$.

label: ex:clone_enrichment
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:clone_enrichment}
Recall that clones may be identified with 
monoids in $[\mathbf{F},\mathbf{Set}]$ with the substitution monoidal structure.
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a locally small\footnote{Recall that by 
Convention~\ref{conv:size}, ``locally small'' implies ``large''.} 
category with all finite powers.
We have an enrichment of $\mathcal{C}$ over $[\mathbf{F},\mathbf{Set}]$ defined as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item The functor ${\langle -, -\rangle}\colon \mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}
\longrightarrow[\mathbf{F},\mathbf{Set}]$
maps $A,B\in\mathcal{C}$ and $[n]\in\mathbf{F}$ to the set 
\[
{\langle A, B\rangle}_n=\mathcal{C}(A^n,B).
\]
\item The natural transformation $(j_C\colon I\longrightarrow 
{\langle C, C\rangle})_{C\in\mathcal{C}}$ corresponds by the Yoneda lemma
(recall that $I=\mathbf{F}([1],-)$) to the family 
\[
(\overline{j}_C={\mathrm{id}_{C}}\in {\langle C, C\rangle}_1)_{C\in\mathcal{C}}.
\] 
\item The natural transformation $(M_{A,B,C}\colon {\langle B, C\rangle}\otimes
{\langle A, B\rangle}\longrightarrow{\langle A, C\rangle})_{A,B,C\in\mathcal{C}}$
corresponds by the universality of coends (recall
that $(Y\otimes X)_{n}=\int^{[k]\in\mathbf{F}} Y_k\times (X_n)^k$) to 
the family whose $(A,B,C)$-th component is given by
\[
(\overline{M}_{A,B,C})_{n,k}\colon {\langle B, C\rangle}_k\times ({\langle A, B\rangle}_n)^k
\longrightarrow{\langle A, B\rangle}_n
\]
mapping $(g,f_1,\dots,f_k)\in \mathcal{C}(B^k,C)\times \mathcal{C}(A^n,B)^k$
to $g\circ\langle f_1,\dots,f_k\rangle\in\mathcal{C}(A^n,B)$.
\end{itemize}

Clearly the definition of the clone $\mathsf{End}(A)$ from a set $A$ 
(Definition~\ref{def:endo_clone}) is derived from the above enrichment,
by setting $\mathcal{C}=\mathbf{Set}$.
Consequently, we restore the classical definitions of model 
(Definition~\ref{def:clone_model})
and homomorphism between models (Definition~\ref{def:clone_mod_hom}) for clones
as instances of Definition~\ref{def:enrich_model}.

title: Example
body_md:
Symmetric operads may be identified with 
monoids in $[\mathbf{P},\mathbf{Set}]$ with the substitution monoidal structure.
Let $\mathcal{C}=(\mathcal{C},I',\otimes')$ 
be a locally small symmetric monoidal category.
We have an enrichment of $\mathcal{C}$ over $[\mathbf{P},\mathbf{Set}]$ defined as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item The functor ${\langle -, -\rangle}\colon \mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}
\longrightarrow[\mathbf{P},\mathbf{Set}]$
maps $A,B\in\mathcal{C}$ and $[n]\in\mathbf{P}$ to the set 
\[
{\langle A, B\rangle}_n=\mathcal{C}(A^{\otimes' n},B),
\]
where $A^{\otimes' n}$ is the monoidal product of $n$ many copies of $A$.
\item The natural transformation $(j_C\colon I\longrightarrow 
{\langle C, C\rangle})_{C\in\mathcal{C}}$ corresponds by the Yoneda lemma
(recall that $I=\mathbf{P}([1],-)$) to the family 
\[
(\overline{j}_C={\mathrm{id}_{C}}\in {\langle C, C\rangle}_1)_{C\in\mathcal{C}}.
\] 
\item The natural transformation $(M_{A,B,C}\colon {\langle B, C\rangle}\otimes
{\langle A, B\rangle}\longrightarrow{\langle A, C\rangle})_{A,B,C\in\mathcal{C}}$
corresponds by the universality of coends (recall 
Definition~\ref{def:subst_monoidal_P}) to 
the family whose $(A,B,C)$-th component is given by
\begin{multline*}
(\overline{M}_{A,B,C})_{n,k,n_1,\dots,n_k}\colon 
{\langle B, C\rangle}_k\times \mathbf{P}([n_1+\dots+n_k],[n])\\ \times
{\langle A, B\rangle}_{n_1}\times\dots\times{\langle A, B\rangle}_{n_k}
\longrightarrow{\langle A, B\rangle}_n,
\end{multline*}
which is the unique function from the empty set if $n\neq n_1+\dots+n_k$
and, if $n= n_1+\dots+n_k$, maps 
$(g,u,f_1,\dots,f_k)\in \mathcal{C}(B^{\otimes' k},C)\times 
\mathbf{P}([n_1+\dots+n_k],[n])\times \mathcal{C}(A^{\otimes' n_1},B)
\times\dots\times \mathcal{C}(A^{\otimes' n_k},B)$
to $g\circ (f_1\otimes'\dots\otimes' f_k)\circ A^{\otimes' u}$.
\end{itemize}

Via the above enrichment, we restore the classical definitions of model and 
homomorphism between models for symmetric operads.

monoids in $[\mathbf{N},\mathbf{Set}]$ with the substitution monoidal structure.

label: ex:relative_alg
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:relative_alg}
We may also consider infinitary variants of Example~\ref{ex:clone_enrichment}.
Here we take an extreme. 
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a locally small category with all small powers. 
Then we obtain an enrichment of $\mathcal{C}$ over $[\mathbf{Set},\mathbf{Set}]$,
the category of endofunctors on $\mathbf{Set}$ with composition as the monoidal product.
\begin{itemize}
\item The functor ${\langle -, -\rangle}\colon \mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times 
\mathcal{C}\longrightarrow[\mathbf{Set},\mathbf{Set}]$ maps $A,B\in\mathcal{C}$
and $X\in \mathbf{Set}$ to the set 
\[
{\langle A, B\rangle}(X)=\mathcal{C}(A^X,B),
\]
where $A^X$ is the $X$-th power of $A$.
\item The natural transformation $(j_C\colon {\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{Set}}}\longrightarrow 
{\langle C, C\rangle})_{C\in\mathcal{C}}$ corresponds by the Yoneda lemma
(note that ${\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{Set}}}\cong\mathbf{Set}(1,-)$, where $1$ is a singleton)
to the family
\[
(\overline{j}_C={\mathrm{id}_{C}}\in{\langle C, C\rangle}(1))_{C\in\mathcal{C}}.
\]
\item The natural transformation $(M_{A,B,C}\colon 
{\langle B, C\rangle}\circ{\langle A, B\rangle}\longrightarrow{\langle A, C\rangle})_{A,B,C\in\mathcal{C}}$
has the $X$-th component ($X\in\mathbf{Set}$)
\[
{\langle B, C\rangle}\circ{\langle A, B\rangle}(X)=\mathcal{C}(B^{\mathcal{C}(A^X,B)},C)\longrightarrow
\mathcal{C}(A^X,C)={\langle A, C\rangle}(X)
\]
the function induced from the canonical morphism $A^X\longrightarrow 
B^{\mathcal{C}(A^X,B)}$ in $\mathcal{C}$.
\end{itemize}

Since monoids in $[\mathbf{Set},\mathbf{Set}]$ are precisely monads on $\mathbf{Set}$,
this enrichment gives us a definition of model of a monad $\mathsf{T}$
on $\mathbf{Set}$ in $\mathcal{C}$. 
To spell this out, first note that 
for any object $C\in\mathcal{C}$, the functor ${\langle C, C\rangle}\colon 
\mathbf{Set}\longrightarrow\mathbf{Set}$ which maps $X\in\mathbf{Set}$ to $\mathcal{C}(C^X,C)$
acquires the monad structure, giving rise to the monad $\mathsf{End}_{{\langle -, -\rangle}}(C)$
on $\mathbf{Set}$.
A model of $\mathsf{T}$ is then an object $C\in\mathcal{C}$ together with
a monad morphism $\mathsf{T}\longrightarrow\mathsf{End}_{{\langle -, -\rangle}}(C)$.
This is the definition of \emph{relative algebra} of a monad on $\mathbf{Set}$ by 
Hino, Kobayashi, Hasuo and Jacobs~\cite{Hino}.
As noted in \cite{Hino}, in the case where $\mathcal{C}=\mathbf{Set}$,
relative algebras of a monad $\mathsf{T}$ on $\mathbf{Set}$ agree with Eilenberg--Moore 
algebras of $\mathsf{T}$; we shall later show this fact
in Example~\ref{ex:monad_on_cat_w_powers}.

\begin{itemize}

G\Longrightarrow G'$ and an $\mathcal{M}$-natural transformation $\phi\colon 
H\Longrightarrow H'$ such that $\phi_0\circ J=J'\circ \theta$.\qedhere
\end{itemize}

label: ex:monad_on_cat_w_powers
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:monad_on_cat_w_powers}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a locally small category with all small powers.
Recall the strict action
\[
\ast\colon[\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C}]\times\mathcal{C}\longrightarrow\mathcal{C}
\]
of the monoidal category $[\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C}]$ of endofunctors on $\mathcal{C}$
on $\mathcal{C}$, used to capture Eilenberg--Moore algebras of monads
on $\mathcal{C}$.
For any object $C\in\mathcal{C}$, write by ${\lceil C\rceil}\colon 1\longrightarrow\mathcal{C}$
the functor from the terminal category $1$ which maps the unique object of $1$
to $C\in\mathcal{C}$ (${\lceil C\rceil}$ is sometimes called the \emph{name of $C$}).

By the assumptions on $\mathcal{C}$,
for any object $A\in\mathcal{C}$ the functor $-\ast A$ (which may be seen as
the precomposition by ${\lceil A\rceil}\colon 1\longrightarrow\mathcal{C}$) admits
a right adjoint ${\langle A, -\rangle}$, which maps any $B\in\mathcal{C}$ (equivalently,
${\lceil B\rceil}\colon 1\longrightarrow\mathcal{C}$) to the right Kan extension 
${\langle A, B\rangle}=\mathrm{Ran}_{{\lceil A\rceil}}{\lceil B\rceil}$ of ${\lceil B\rceil}$ along ${\lceil A\rceil}$.
The functor $\mathrm{Ran}_{{\lceil A\rceil}}{\lceil B\rceil}\colon\mathcal{C}\longrightarrow\mathcal{C}$
maps $C\in\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathrm{Ran}_{{\lceil A\rceil}}{\lceil B\rceil}(C)=B^{\mathcal{C}(C,A)}$.

For any object $C\in\mathcal{C}$, $\mathrm{Ran}_{{\lceil C\rceil}}{\lceil C\rceil}$
exists and becomes a monad on $\mathcal{C}$ in a canonical way (the \emph{codensity 
monad of ${\lceil C\rceil}$}).
For any monad $\mathsf{T}$ on $\mathcal{C}$, to give a structure of an 
Eilenberg--Moore algebra on $C\in\mathcal{C}$ is equivalent to 
give a monad morphism from $\mathsf{T}$ to $\mathrm{Ran}_{{\lceil C\rceil}}{\lceil C\rceil}$.
This observation is in e.g., \cite[Section~3]{Kelly_coherence_lax_dist}.

In particular, if we take $\mathcal{C}=\mathbf{Set}$,
we see that the above enrichment agrees with the one given 
in Example~\ref{ex:relative_alg}.
Hence the notion of relative algebra \cite{Hino} agrees with
that of Eilenberg--Moore algebra in this case.

body_md:
\label{def:profunctor}
We define the bicategory ${\mathscr{P\!R\!O\!F}}$ as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item An object is a large category.
\item A 1-cell from $\mathcal{A}$ to $\mathcal{B}$ is a \textbf{profunctor from 
$\mathcal{A}$ to $\mathcal{B}$}, which we define to be 
a functor 
\[
H\colon \mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{A}\longrightarrow\mathbf{SET}.
\]
We write $H\colon \mathcal{A}\mathrel{\mathpalette\p@to@gets\to}\mathcal{B}$ if $H$ is a profunctor from $\mathcal{A}$
to $\mathcal{B}$.
The identity 1-cell on a large category $\mathcal{C}$
is the hom-functor $\mathcal{C}(-,-)$.
Given profunctors $H\colon \mathcal{A}\mathrel{\mathpalette\p@to@gets\to}\mathcal{B}$ and $K\colon \mathcal{B}\mathrel{\mathpalette\p@to@gets\to}\mathcal{C}$,
their composite 
$K\odot H\colon\mathcal{A}\mathrel{\mathpalette\p@to@gets\to}\mathcal{C}$ maps $(C,A)\in\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{A}$
to 
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:profunctor_composition}
(K\odot H)(C,A)=\int^{B\in\mathcal{B}} K(C,B)\times H(B,A).
\end{equation}
\item A 2-cell from $H$ to $H'$, both from $\mathcal{A}$ to $\mathcal{B}$,
is a natural transformation $\alpha\colon H\Longrightarrow H'
\colon\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{A}\longrightarrow\mathbf{SET}$.\qedhere
\end{itemize}

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a large category. 
Define the monoidal category $[\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times \mathcal{C},\mathbf{SET}]
=([\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C},\mathbf{SET}],\mathcal{C}(-,-),\mathbin{\odot^\mathrm{rev}})$ of
\textbf{endo-profunctors on $\mathcal{C}$}
to be the endo-hom-category ${\mathscr{P\!R\!O\!F}}^{\mathrm{op}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C})$.
More precisely:
\begin{itemize}
\item The unit object is the hom-functor
$\mathcal{C}(-,-)\colon \mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\longrightarrow\mathbf{SET}$.
\item Given $H,K\colon\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\longrightarrow\mathbf{SET}$,
define their monoidal product $H\mathbin{\odot^\mathrm{rev}} K$
to be the functor which maps $(A,C)\in\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}$ to
\[
(H\mathbin{\odot^\mathrm{rev}} K)(A,C)=\int^{B\in\mathcal{C}}H(B,C)\times K(A,B).\qedhere
\]
\end{itemize}

$1$  to ${j_C}$).

$(\overline{\phi}_{X,Y})_{A,B,C}\colon 
\Phi_Y(B,C)\times\Phi_X(A,B)
\longrightarrow\Phi_{Y\otimes X}(A,C)$

profunctors $H$ and $K$ (Definition~\ref{def:profunctor}), and 
$k_\cdot \odot h_\cdot$ and $k\odot h$ are the evident
natural transformations.

$\alpha\colon H\Longrightarrow 
H'\colon\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{M}\longrightarrow\mathbf{SET}$. \qedhere

in $\mathcal{C}$.
We define the metamodel 
$H(\Phi)=(\Phi',\overline{\phi'}_\cdot,\overline{\phi'})$ 
of $\mathcal{N}$ on $\mathcal{C}$ as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item The functor 
$\Phi'\colon\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\longrightarrow\mathbf{SET}$
maps $(N,A,B)\in\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}$ to the set 
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:action_of_H_on_metamodels}
\Phi'_N(A,B)=
\int^{M\in\mathcal{M}}H(N,M)\times \Phi_M(A,B).
\end{equation}
\item The natural transformation $((\overline{\phi'}_\cdot)_C\colon 
1\longrightarrow \Phi'_{I_\mathcal{N}}(C,C))_{C\in\mathcal{C}}$
is defined by
mapping the unique element $\ast$ of $1$ to
\begin{multline*}
[I_\mathcal{M}\in\mathcal{M}, h_\cdot(\ast)\in H(I_\mathcal{N},I_\mathcal{M}), 
(\overline{\phi}_\cdot)_C(\ast)\in
\Phi_{I_\mathcal{M}}(C,C)]\\
\in\int^{M\in\mathcal{M}}H(I_\mathcal{N},M)\times \Phi_M(C,C)
\end{multline*}
for each $C\in\mathcal{C}$. 
\item The natural transformation 
\[((\overline{\phi'}_{N,N'})_{A,B,C}\colon
\Phi'_{N'}(B,C)\times\Phi'_N(A,B)\longrightarrow
\Phi'_{N'\otimes_\mathcal{N} N}(A,C))_{N,N'\in\mathcal{N},A,B,C\in\mathcal{C}}\]
is defined by mapping a pair consisting of
$[M',x',y']\in\Phi'_{N'}(B,C)$ and $[M,x,y]\in\Phi'_N(A,B)$
to 
\begin{equation*}
[M'\otimes_\mathcal{M}M, h_{N,N',M,M'}(x',x), 
(\overline{\phi}_{M,M'})_{A,B,C}(y',y)]
\end{equation*}
for each $N,N'\in\mathcal{N}$ and $A,B,C\in\mathcal{C}$.\qedhere
\end{itemize}

title: Example
body_md:
Let us consider the relationship between clones and monads on $\mathbf{Set}$.
The inclusion functor
\[
J''\colon \mathbf{F}\longrightarrow\mathbf{Set}
\]
induces a functor 
\[
\mathrm{Lan}_{J''}\colon[\mathbf{F},\mathbf{Set}]\longrightarrow[\mathbf{Set},\mathbf{Set}],
\]
which naturally acquires the structure of a strong monoidal functor.
The essential image of this functor is precisely the \emph{finitary}
endofunctors on $\mathbf{Set}$, i.e., those endofunctors preserving filtered colimits.
The functor ${\mathbf{Th}(\mathrm{Lan}_{J''})}$ maps a clone to a finitary monad on $\mathbf{Set}$,
in accordance with 
the well-known correspondence between clones (= Lawvere theories) and finitary 
monads on $\mathbf{Set}$ \cite{Linton_equational}.
Between the 2-categories of metamodels, we have a 2-functor
\[
{\mathscr{M}\!\mathscr{M}\!od((\mathrm{Lan}_{J''})^\ast)}\colon{\mathscr{M}\!\mathscr{M}\!od([\mathbf{Set},\mathbf{Set}])}\longrightarrow
{\mathscr{M}\!\mathscr{M}\!od([\mathbf{F},\mathbf{Set}])}.
\]
The standard metamodel of $[\mathbf{Set},\mathbf{Set}]$ in $\mathbf{Set}$ (corresponding to the 
definition of Eilenberg--Moore algebras) is given by the strict action
described in Example~\ref{ex:monad_standard_action};
in particular, its functor part $\Phi\colon 
[\mathbf{Set},\mathbf{Set}]^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf{Set}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf{Set}\longrightarrow\mathbf{SET}$ maps $(F,A,B)$ to 
$\mathbf{Set}(FA,B)$. 
The metamodel $(\mathrm{Lan}_{J''})^\ast(\Phi)$ of $[\mathbf{F},\mathbf{Set}]$ in $\mathbf{Set}$ has the 
functor part $(\mathrm{Lan}_{J''})^\ast(\Phi)\colon[\mathbf{F},\mathbf{Set}]^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf{Set}^{\mathrm{op}}\times
\mathbf{Set}\longrightarrow\mathbf{SET}$ mapping $(X,A,B)$ to 
\begin{align*}
\mathbf{Set}((\mathrm{Lan}_{J''}X)A,B)
&= \mathbf{Set}\left(\int^{[n]\in\mathbf{F}} A^n\times X_n,B\right)\\
&\cong \int_{[n]\in\mathbf{F}} \mathbf{Set} (X_n, \mathbf{Set}(A^n,B))\\
&\cong [\mathbf{F},\mathbf{Set}] (X, {\langle A, B\rangle}),
\end{align*}
where ${\langle A, B\rangle}\in[\mathbf{F},\mathbf{Set}]$ in the final line is the one in 
Example~\ref{ex:clone_enrichment}.
Hence ${\mathscr{M}\!\mathscr{M}\!od((\mathrm{Lan}_{J''})^\ast)}$ preserves the standard metamodels 
and this way we restore the well-known observation 
that the classical correspondence 
of clones and finitary monads on $\mathbf{Set}$ preserves semantics.

Note that by combining the previous example we obtain the chain
\[
\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline=-\the\dimexpr\fontdimen22\textfont2\relax ]
      \node (L) at (0,0)  {$[\mathbf{N},\mathbf{Set}]$};
      \node (M) at (2.5,0)  {$[\mathbf{P},\mathbf{Set}]$};
      \node (R) at (5,0)  {$[\mathbf{F},\mathbf{Set}]$};
      \node (RR) at (7.5,0) {$[\mathbf{Set},\mathbf{Set}]$};
       
      \draw[->]  (L) to node[auto,labelsize] 
      {$\mathrm{Lan}_J$} (M);
      \draw[->]  (M) to node[auto,labelsize] 
      {$\mathrm{Lan}_{J'}$} (R);
      \draw[->]  (R) to node[auto,labelsize] 
      {$\mathrm{Lan}_{J''}$} (RR);
\end{tikzpicture} 
\] 
of strong monoidal functors, connecting non-symmetric and symmetric operads 
with monads on $\mathbf{Set}$.

title: Example
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a metatheory, $\mathcal{C}$ a large category,
and $\ast$ a \emph{pseudo} action of $\mathcal{M}$ on $\mathcal{C}$.
We obtain a strong monoidal functor 
\[
F\colon\mathcal{M}\longrightarrow[\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C}]
\]
(where $[\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C}]$ is equipped with the composition monoidal structure)
as the transpose of $\ast\colon\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{C}\longrightarrow\mathcal{C}$.
The functor ${\mathbf{Th}(F)}$ maps any theory $\mathsf{T}=(T,e,m)$ in $\mathcal{M}$
to the monad $F(\mathsf{T})=(T\ast(-), e\ast(-),m\ast(-))$ on $\mathcal{C}$.
The 2-functor 
${\mathscr{M}\!\mathscr{M}\!od(F^\ast)}\colon{\mathscr{M}\!\mathscr{M}\!od([\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C}])}\longrightarrow{\mathscr{M}\!\mathscr{M}\!od(\mathcal{M})}$
maps the standard metamodel $\Phi$ of $[\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C}]$ in $\mathcal{C}$
(Example~\ref{ex:monad_standard_action}) to the metamodel 
$F^\ast(\Phi)\colon 
\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\longrightarrow\mathbf{SET}$
mapping $(X,A,B)$ to
\[
\mathcal{C}((FX)A,B)=\mathcal{C}(X\ast A,B).
\]
Therefore it maps the standard metamodel $\Phi$ to the metamodel induced from 
$\ast$.

As a special case, for a large category $\mathcal{C}$ with finite limits and a 
cartesian monad $\mathsf{S}$ on $\mathcal{C}$,
the standard metamodel for $\mathsf{S}$-operads
(Example~\ref{ex:metamodel_S-operad}) may be related to 
the standard metamodel of monads on $\mathcal{C}$,
and models of an $\mathsf{S}$-operad $\mathsf{T}$ may alternatively be defined 
as Eilenberg--Moore algebras of the monad on $\mathcal{C}$ induced from $\mathsf{T}$
(as noted in \cite{Leinster_book}).

First, that $({\mathbf{Mod}(\mathsf{T},\mathcal{C})},U,u)$ is a vertical double cone over 
$\Phi(\mathsf{T})$ follows directly from the definition of model of $\mathsf{T}$
in $\mathcal{C}$ with respect to $\Phi$ (Definition~\ref{def:metamodel_model}).

Given a vertical double cone $(\mathcal{A},V,v)$ over $\Phi(\mathsf{T})$,
for each object $A\in\mathcal{A}$, the pair $(VA,v_{A,A}({\mathrm{id}_{A}}))$ is a
$\mathsf{T}$-model in $\mathcal{C}$ with respect to $\Phi$,
and for each morphism $f\colon A\longrightarrow A'$ in $\mathcal{A}$,
the morphism $Vf$ is a $\mathsf{T}$-model homomorphism from 
$(VA,v_{A,A}({\mathrm{id}_{A}}))$ to $(VA',v_{A',A'}({\mathrm{id}_{A'}}))$.
The functor $K\colon \mathcal{A}\longrightarrow {\mathbf{Mod}(\mathsf{T},\mathcal{C})}$
can therefore be given as $KA=(VA,v_{A,A}({\mathrm{id}_{A}}))$ and $Kf=Vf$.
The uniqueness is clear. 

Finally, given $H$ and $\theta$ as in the third clause, the equation 
(\ref{eqn:H_theta}) says that for each $A\in\mathcal{A}$, $A'\in\mathcal{A'}$ 
and $x\in H(A,A')$, the 
morphism $\theta_{A,A'}(x)\colon VA\longrightarrow V'A'$
in $\mathcal{C}$ satisfies $\Phi_T(VA,\theta_{A,A'}(x)) (v_{A,A}({\mathrm{id}_{A}}))= 
\Phi_T(\theta_{A,A'}(x),VA')(v'_{A',A'}({\mathrm{id}_{A'}}))$;
in other words, that $\theta_{A,A'}(x)$ is a $\mathsf{T}$-model homomorphism
from $KA$ to $K'A'$.
The square $\sigma$ can then be given as the natural transformation 
with $\sigma_{A,A'}(x)=\theta_{A,A'}(x)$.

label: def:simp
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:simp}
We define the \textbf{augmented simplex category} (also known as the
\textbf{algebraists' simplex category})
$\Delta_{a}$ as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item Objects are all finite ordinals $\mathbf{n}=\{\,{0}<{1}<\dots 
<{n-1} \,\}$,
including the empty ordinal $\mathbf{0}=\{\ \}$.
\item Morphisms are all monotone functions.
\end{itemize}
Note that a morphism in $\Delta_{a}$ is mono (resp.~epi)
iff it is an injective (resp.~surjective) monotone function.

This category has a natural monoidal structure, given as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item The unit object is $\mathbf{0}$.
\item The monoidal product $+\colon 
\Delta_{a}\times\Delta_{a}\longrightarrow\Delta_{a}$ maps a pair of objects 
$\mathbf{n}$ and $\mathbf{m}$ in $\Delta_{a}$ to $\mathbf{n+m}$, and maps a pair of morphisms 
$u\colon \mathbf{n}\longrightarrow \mathbf{n'}$ and 
$v\colon \mathbf{m}\longrightarrow\mathbf{m'}$ in $\Delta_{a}$ to 
$u+v\colon \mathbf{n+m}\longrightarrow\mathbf{n'+m'}$ defined as
\[
(u+v) ({i}) =\begin{cases}
u(i) & \text{if }i\leq n-1\\
n'+v(i) & \text{if }i\geq n.
\end{cases}
\]
\end{itemize}
In the following, whenever we talk about a monoidal structure on $\Delta_{a}$,
we always mean this (strict) monoidal structure $(\mathbf{0},+)$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{M},I,\otimes)$ be a metatheory.
There is an equivalence of categories 
between the category ${\mathscr{M}\!on\mathscr{C\!A\!T}_{\mathrm{strong}}}(\Delta_{a},\mathcal{M})$ of all strong monoidal functors
$\Delta_{a}\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}$ and monoidal natural transformations,
and the category ${\mathbf{Th}(\mathcal{M})}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that a strong monoidal functor $(F,f_\cdot,f)\colon 
\Delta_{a}\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}$ consists of a functor $F\colon 
\Delta_{a}\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}$, an isomorphism $f_\cdot\colon I\longrightarrow 
F(\mathbf{0})$ and a natural isomorphism 
\[
f=(f_{\mathbf{m},\mathbf{n}}\colon F(\mathbf{n})\otimes F(\mathbf{m})\longrightarrow 
F(\mathbf{n+m}))_{\mathbf{m},\mathbf{n}\in\Delta_{a}}
\]
satisfying the suitable axioms. The functor
\[
{\mathscr{M}\!on\mathscr{C\!A\!T}_{\mathrm{strong}}}(\Delta_{a},\mathcal{M})\longrightarrow {\mathbf{Th}(\mathcal{M})}
\]
mapping an object $(F,f_\cdot,f)\in{\mathscr{M}\!on\mathscr{C\!A\!T}_{\mathrm{strong}}}(\Delta_{a},\mathcal{M})$ to $(F(\mathbf{1}),
F({!_\mathbf{0}})\circ f_\cdot, F({!_{\mathbf{2}}})\circ 
f_{\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}})$
and a morphism $\phi\colon (F,f_\cdot,f)\longrightarrow (G,g_\cdot,g)$
in ${\mathscr{M}\!on\mathscr{C\!A\!T}_{\mathrm{strong}}}(\Delta_{a},\mathcal{M})$ to $\phi_\mathbf{1}$ 
is well-defined and is an equivalence of categories.

together with, for each $x,y\in{\mathrm{ob}(G)}$,

products, the category ${{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Cat}}^{(n)}$

$n$-dimensional $\mathcal{V}$-category} (to avoid confusion with \emph{weak} 
$n$-dimensional $\mathcal{V}$-category which we are trying to define).

label: prop:VGph_ext
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The coproduct of a family $(G_i)_{i\in I}$ 
of $\mathcal{V}$-graphs is given by
${\mathrm{ob}(\coprod_{i\in I}G_i)}=\coprod_{i\in I}{\mathrm{ob}(G_i)}$
and 
\[
(\coprod_{i\in I}G_i) ((i,x), (i',x'))=
\begin{cases}
G_i(x,x')\quad &\text{if }i=i',\\
0&\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
It is easy to see that
the functor $\coprod\colon \prod_{i\in I}({{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}/G_i)\longrightarrow
{{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}/(\coprod_{i\in I}G_i)$
(as in~(\ref{eqn:ext_coprod})) is full and faithful.
For any object $(f\colon H\longrightarrow \coprod_{i\in I}G_i)$
in ${{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}/{(\coprod_{i\in I} G_i)}$,
define an object $(f_i\colon H_i\longrightarrow G_i)_{i\in I}\in \prod_{i\in 
I}(\mathcal{V}/G_i)$
by the pullbacks
of $f$ along the coprojections $\sigma_i\colon G_i\longrightarrow \coprod_{i\in 
I}G_i$;
note that these pullbacks always exist, 
and $H_i$ are just the suitable ``full sub'' $\mathcal{V}$-graphs
of $H$.
Since $0$ is strict, 
$(\coprod_{i\in I}f_i \colon \coprod_{i\in I}H_i\longrightarrow 
\coprod_{i\in 
I}G_i)$
is isomorphic to $f$. Hence $\coprod$ is also essentially surjective.

label: prop:VCat_ext
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Coproducts in ${{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Cat}}$ are formed just as in ${{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}$;
namely, given a family $(\mathcal{C}_i)_{i\in I}$ of $\mathcal{V}$-categories, 
we have ${\mathrm{ob}(\coprod_{i\in I} \mathcal{C}_i)}=\coprod_{i\in I} {\mathrm{ob}(\mathcal{C}_i)}$
and 
\[
(\coprod_{i\in I}\mathcal{C}_i) ((i,x), (i',x'))=
\begin{cases}
\mathcal{C}_i(x,x')\quad &\text{if }i=i',\\
0&\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
Note that to define a composition law for $\coprod_{i\in I}\mathcal{C}_i$, we use 
the fact that for a category $\mathcal{V}$ with a strict initial object $0$,
$0\times B\cong 0$ for every object $B\in\mathcal{V}$.\footnote{In fact, for a 
category $\mathcal{V}$ with an initial object $0$ and finite products, $0$ is 
strict if and only if $0\times B\cong 0$ for 
every $B\in \mathcal{V}$.}
The rest of the proof is identical to that of Proposition~\ref{prop:VGph_ext}.

label: prop:free_V_cat
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:free_V_cat}
If $\mathcal{V}$ has finite products and small coproducts, and if 
for any $B\in\mathcal{V}$ the functor $(-)\times B\colon
\mathcal{V}\longrightarrow \mathcal{V}$ preserves small coproducts, then the
forgetful functor
$U\colon{{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Cat}}\longrightarrow{{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}$ admits a left
adjoint $F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Given a $\mathcal{V}$-graph $G=({\mathrm{ob}(G)},(G(x,y))_{x,y\in{\mathrm{ob}(G)}})$, the free 
$\mathcal{V}$-category $FG$ on $G$ 
has the same objects as $G$ and the hom-object given by
\[
(FG)(x,y)=\coprod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\coprod_{\substack{w_0,\dots,w_n\in 
{\mathrm{ob}(G)}\\w_0=x,w_n=y}}G(w_{n-1},w_{n})\times\cdots\times G(w_0,w_1)
\]
for all $x,y\in {\mathrm{ob}(FG)}={\mathrm{ob}(G)}$.
To spell out the identity elements and composition laws in $FG$, let us write 
\[
(FG)(x,y)_n=\coprod_{\substack{w_0,\dots,w_n\in 
{\mathrm{ob}(G)}\\w_0=x,w_n=y}}G(w_{n-1},w_{n})\times\cdots\times G(w_0,w_1) 
\]
for all $x,y\in{\mathrm{ob}(FG)}$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$.

Note that $(FG)(x,y)_0$ is the terminal object $1$ of $\mathcal{V}$ if $x=y$
(otherwise, it is the initial object $0$ of $\mathcal{V}$).
Hence the identity element on $x\in{\mathrm{ob}(FG)}$ can be given as 
\[
\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline=-\the\dimexpr\fontdimen22\textfont2\relax ]
      \node            (0) {$1$};
      \node[right=of 0](1) {$(FG)(x,x)_0$};
      \node[right=of 1](d) 
      {$\coprod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}(FG)(x,x)_n=(FG)(x,y)$,};
      
      \draw [->] (0) to node [auto,labelsize] {$\cong$} (1);
      \draw [->] (1) to node [auto,labelsize] {$\sigma_0$} (d);
\end{tikzpicture}
\]
where $\sigma_0$ denotes the $0$-th coprojection.
Given any triple $x,y,z\in{\mathrm{ob}(FG)}$ of objects, by the assumption we have 
\[
(FG)(y,z)\times (FG)(x,y)\cong \coprod_{k,l\in\mathbb{N}}(FG)(y,z)_l\times (FG)(x,y)_k.
\]
Using the assumption once again, we see that $(FG)(y,z)_l\times (FG)(x,y)_k$
is isomorphic to 
\[
\coprod_{\substack{u_0,\dots,u_k,v_0,\dots,v_l\in {\mathrm{ob}(G)}\\
u_0=x,u_k=v_0=y,v_l=z}}G(v_{l-1},v_l)\times\dots\times G(v_0,v_1)\times
G(u_{k-1},u_k)\times\dots\times G(u_0,u_1),
\]
and therefore naturally embeds into $(FG)(x,z)_{k+l}$.
The universality of coproducts induce the composition laws for $FG$ from these 
embeddings.

adjoint) and $F$ (by Proposition~\ref{prop:free_V_cat_pres_pb}) do.

The multiplication $\mu=U\varepsilon F$ is cartesian because $\varepsilon F$ 
is so by Proposition~\ref{prop:free_V_cat_counit} (take $m=1$), 
and $U$ preserves pullbacks.

{{({{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Cat}}^{(n)})}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}$ is cartesian by
Proposition~\ref{prop:free_V_cat_unit}.

title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defn:generating_cofibrations}
Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a category with a terminal object and finite coproducts.
For each natural number $n$, define a family
$\mathcal{F}^{(n)}=(f^{(n)}_0,\dots,f^{(n)}_{n+1})$
of morphisms in ${{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}^{(n)}$ recursively as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $f^{(0)}_0\colon 0\longrightarrow 1$ and 
$f^{(0)}_1\colon 1+1\longrightarrow 1$ are the unique morphisms in $\mathcal{V}$
into the terminal object $1$.
\item $f^{(n)}_0\colon D\emptyset \longrightarrow D\{\ast\}$,
where $\emptyset$ and $\{\ast\}$ are the empty set and a singleton
respectively,
is the unique morphism in ${{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}^{(n)}$ 
out of the initial object $D\emptyset$,
and for each $i\in \{1,\dots, n+1\}$,
$f^{(n)}_i=\Sigma f^{(n-1)}_{i-1}$.\qedhere
\end{enumerate}

title: Theorem
body_md:
If $\mathcal{V}$ is a locally presentable and extensive category,
then for any natural number $n$
the category ${T^{(n)}}\mhyphen{\mathbf{OC}}$ has an initial object.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We shall follow the argument in \cite[Appendix~G]{Leinster_book} 
(where $\mathcal{V}=\mathbf{Set}$ and $n=\omega$) and 
                                    
show that ${{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}^{(n)}/T^{(n)}1$ is locally presentable
(hence is both complete and cocomplete), and that $W$ and $V_{T^{(n)}1}$
are monadic and accessible. 
Then by \cite[Theorem~27.1]{Kelly_unified} it follows that the 
forgetful functor from ${\mathsf{T}^{(n)}}\mhyphen{\mathbf{OC}}$ to 
${{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}^{(n)}/T^{(n)}1$
(the composite of functors in (\ref{eqn:pb_OC}))
is also monadic, thus in particular
${\mathsf{T}^{(n)}}\mhyphen{\mathbf{OC}}$ has an initial object, given by the 
free algebra over the initial object in ${{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}^{(n)}/T^{(n)}1$.

Because ${{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}^{(n)}$ is locally 
presentable,
so is ${{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}^{(n)}/T^{(n)}1$, being its slice.
The functor $W$ is monadic because it is the forgetful functor from a 
category of monoids and admits a left adjoint $G$
(which, incidentally, is of a particularly simple form 
$GP=\coprod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}P^{\otimes n}$
thanks to Proposition~\ref{prop:forgetful_n_pres_coprod}).
It is routine to show that $W$ is accessible.
The functor $V_{T^{(n)}1}$ is monadic and accessible by 
Proposition~\ref{prop:V_X_monadic_accessible}.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a locally presentable extensive category and $n$ be a natural
number.
A \textbf{weak $n$-dimensional $\mathcal{V}$-category} is 
a model of the initial $\mathsf{T}^{(n)}$-operad with contraction,
where $\mathsf{T}^{(n)}$ is the free strict $n$-dimensional $\mathcal{V}$-category
monad on ${{\mathcal{V}}\mhyphen\mathbf{Gph}}^{(n)}$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
If we let $\mathcal{V}=\mathbf{Set}$ and $n=2$,
then weak $2$-categories (weak $2$-dimensional $\mathbf{Set}$-categories) 
are equivalent to \emph{unbiased bicategories},
which are a variant of bicategories
equipped with for each natural number $m$, an $m$-ary horizontal
composition operation. 
See \cite[Section~9.4]{Leinster_book} for details.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
If we let $\mathcal{V}=\omega\mhyphen\mathbf{Cpo}$ and $n=2$, then 
weak $2$-dimensional $\omega\mhyphen\mathbf{Cpo}$-categories
are the unbiased version of $\omega\mhyphen\mathbf{Cpo}$-enriched
bicategories as in \cite{Power_Tanaka}.
